standard.title: European Contact and Impact on First Nations Peoples
standard.description: the causes and effects of European contact and extension of settlement, including their impact on the First Nations Peoples of Australia
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have studied colonial-era Australian history at primary level. In Year 8, they examined the features, power structures, and turning points of pre-modern societies. They have some familiarity with the concept of contact between cultures from earlier years. They have not yet examined the causes of British colonisation of Australia in depth, nor systematically studied the range of impacts on First Nations Australians including frontier conflict, the Stolen Generations, and land dispossession.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students examine the causes and effects of European contact and extension of settlement in Australia, including their impact on First Nations Peoples, and explain the range of responses and experiences.

nodes.label: Causes and legal basis of British colonisation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the causes of European contact and initial settlement of Australia, including the legal and ideological basis of British territorial claims.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least two causes of British colonisation of Australia and identify the legal doctrine used to justify territorial claims.
nodes.typical_width: Examine Cook's instructions from the Admiralty regarding obtaining 'Consent of the Natives'; explain the concept of terra nullius and how it was used to justify British claims; describe the causes of British colonisation including strategic, economic, and social factors (convict transportation as a solution to prison overcrowding, expansion of empire, commercial interests).
wider: Examine Cook's 'secret instructions' as a primary source — identifying the gap between the instruction to obtain Native consent and the actual practice of colonisation — and assess what this reveals about the ideology of empire
Investigate how the legal fiction of terra nullius was later overturned by the Mabo decision (1992) to examine how contemporary legal and political change can reframe historical understanding

Compare British colonial claims in Australia with those in other colonised territories to assess whether the legal and ideological framework of terra nullius was unique to Australia or part of a broader colonial pattern
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding terra nullius and the ideological basis of British settlement is essential context for all subsequent effects and responses. Without it, students will understand frontier conflict and dispossession as isolated events rather than as consequences of a deliberate colonial structure.

response_modes.reason: Students need to understand terra nullius as an ideological and legal construct — not just a fact — before they can analyse its consequences. Invest in explicit reasoning about how legal fictions shape historical outcomes.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two causes of British colonisation of Australia
Explains what terra nullius was and how it was used to justify British territorial claims

nodes.label: Effects of colonisation — conflict, disease, and cultural destruction
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine the effects of European colonisation on First Nations Australians including frontier conflict, massacres, disease, dispossession, removal from land, and relocation to protectorates, reserves and missions.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least two distinct effects of European colonisation on First Nations Australians.
nodes.typical_width: Examine the effects of colonisation including frontier warfare and massacres, the spread of European diseases and its demographic impact, dispossession of land, and the relocation of First Nations Australians to 'protectorates', reserves and missions; analyse how these effects were interconnected and how they changed across the period of colonisation.
wider: Investigate the scale of frontier conflict using available historical evidence — including recent scholarly work on massacre sites — and examine why this history was suppressed in earlier Australian historiography
Examine the demographic impact of introduced diseases on First Nations Australians, comparing documented population estimates before and after colonisation in specific regions

Investigate the reserve and mission system — how it operated, what conditions were like for First Nations Australians, and how it both destroyed and also sometimes preserved certain cultural practices
nodes.hinge_reason: Students must have a substantive understanding of the range and scale of colonisation's effects before they can understand First Nations responses (Node 3) or the Stolen Generations (Node 4). Without this, responses seem disproportionate and the Stolen Generations appears as an isolated event rather than part of a continuing pattern.

response_modes.reason: Using multiple effect types (conflict, disease, dispossession, relocation) prevents students from reducing colonial impact to a single dimension. Each type reveals a different mechanism through which colonisation operated.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The effects of colonisation on First Nations Australians represent one of the most significant and contested areas of Australian history. There is rich material for examining how historical understanding has changed over time (e.g. frontier wars historiography) and for connecting historical events to contemporary reconciliation debates.
success_criteria: Examines at least three distinct effects of colonisation on First Nations Australians with specific historical examples
Explains how at least two effects were connected or compounding

nodes.label: First Nations responses to colonisation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate how First Nations Australians responded to colonisation, including through resistance, economic contribution, cultural adaptation, and engagement with new institutions.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least two different ways First Nations Australians responded to colonisation.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate how First Nations Australians responded to colonisation through: resistance and frontier warfare; making contributions to colonial industries (pastoral, pearling, fishing, farming); adopting Christian practices or attending missions; maintaining cultural practices where possible; and forms of both accommodation and resistance.
wider: Examine specific documented cases of First Nations resistance (e.g. Pemulwuy, Jandamarra, Yagan) to give concrete historical grounding to the concept of frontier resistance
Investigate the role of First Nations Australians in the pastoral industry — examining the conditions under which they worked and the degree to which this represents agency, exploitation, or both

Examine how First Nations Australians engaged with Christianity — exploring cases where adoption of Christian practice was used to maintain community cohesion or resist cultural destruction, not only as a form of assimilation

response_modes.reason: Presenting multiple response types — resistance, economic contribution, cultural adaptation — is essential to avoid a passive or victim-only framing and to represent the full range of First Nations agency.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: This node enables students to engage with First Nations agency — a historically significant corrective to narratives that present First Nations Australians as passive recipients of colonisation. The material is rich, complex, and connects to contemporary debates about historical representation.
success_criteria: Investigates at least two different types of First Nations response to colonisation, with specific examples
Identifies at least one response that demonstrates First Nations agency or resistance, not only accommodation

nodes.label: Forcible removal of children and the Stolen Generations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate the forcible removal of First Nations Australian children, including the motivations, practices, laws, and experiences of separation, and explain how this connects to the broader patterns of colonisation.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the forcible removal of First Nations children — what it involved, why it occurred, and one effect on those removed.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate the forcible removal of First Nations children in the late 19th and 20th centuries including: motivations (assimilationist ideology, 'protection' policies); practices and laws that enabled removal; the geographic and temporal scale of the policy; and the experiences of children and families who were separated. Connect the Stolen Generations to the broader colonial project of cultural destruction examined in Node 2.
wider: Examine the Bringing Them Home Report (1997) as a key document in recognising the Stolen Generations, and assess how its findings changed public understanding of this history
Investigate survivor testimonies from the Stolen Generations to examine the human experience behind the policy — considering both the immediate trauma of removal and its intergenerational effects

Examine how the motivations behind child removal (assimilationist ideology, 'protection' ideology) were consistent with broader colonial approaches to First Nations Australians — connecting Stolen Generations to the reserve system and frontier dispossession as parts of the same ideological framework

response_modes.reason: This node integrates the colonial ideology (Node 1), the pattern of colonial impacts (Node 2), and First Nations responses (Node 3) into the specific case of the Stolen Generations — ensuring students see it as part of a continuous colonial story, not an isolated policy.

success_criteria: Explains the motivations, practices, and laws behind the forcible removal of First Nations children
Describes at least one type of experience of those who were removed, drawing on historical evidence
